summary.text: Both quantities are one plus the number of breakpoints between consecutive ordered divisors, so it suffices to identify their breakpoint conditions. For consecutive divisors \(x<y\), “\(y\) odd and \(y\ge 2x\)” is equivalent to \(y>2x\): equality is incompatible with oddness, while if \(y>2x\) and \(y=2m\), then \(m\mid n\) and \(x<m<y\), contradicting consecutiveness.

full_proof.text:
Let \(n\ge 1\), and write the positive divisors of \(n\) in strictly increasing order as
\[
  d_1<d_2<\cdots<d_r.
\]
This list is nonempty because \(1\mid n\).

We use the following characterization of A237271 in terms of consecutive divisors. It is the divisor formula for the number of parts in the symmetric representation of \(\sigma(n)\):
\[
 a(n)
 =1+\#\bigl\{i:1\le i<r,\ d_{i+1}\text{ is odd and }d_{i+1}\ge 2d_i\bigr\}.
 \tag{1}
\]
Thus, to prove the conjecture, it is enough to relate the condition counted in (1) to the places at which the ordered divisor list fails to be \(2\)-dense.

We first prove the key local assertion.

**Lemma.** If \(x<y\) are consecutive divisors of \(n\), then
\[
  \bigl(y\text{ is odd and }y\ge 2x\bigr)
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  y>2x.
  \tag{2}
\]
Here “consecutive” means that there is no divisor of \(n\) strictly between \(x\) and \(y\).

**Proof of the lemma.** Suppose first that \(y\) is odd and \(y\ge 2x\). Equality \(y=2x\) is impossible, because \(2x\) is even whereas \(y\) is odd. Therefore the inequality must be strict, so \(y>2x\).

Conversely, suppose that \(y>2x\). Certainly this implies \(y\ge 2x\), so it remains only to prove that \(y\) is odd. Assume for contradiction that \(y\) is even. Then we can write
\[
 y=2m
\]
for a positive integer \(m\). Since \(y\mid n\), there is an integer \(q\) such that \(n=yq=2mq\), and hence \(m\mid n\). Thus \(m\) is itself a divisor of \(n\).

The strict inequality \(y>2x\), together with \(y=2m\), gives
\[
 2m>2x,
\]
so \(m>x\). On the other hand, \(m>0\), and therefore
\[
 m<2m=y.
\]
Consequently \(m\) is a divisor of \(n\) strictly between \(x\) and \(y\), contradicting the assumption that \(x\) and \(y\) are consecutive divisors. Hence \(y\) cannot be even and must be odd. This proves (2). \(\square\)

Apply the lemma to every consecutive pair \((d_i,d_{i+1})\). For each \(i<r\), it gives
\[
 \bigl(d_{i+1}\text{ is odd and }d_{i+1}\ge 2d_i\bigr)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 d_{i+1}>2d_i.
 \tag{3}
\]
Therefore the set counted in (1) is exactly the set
\[
 B=\bigl\{i:1\le i<r,\ d_{i+1}>2d_i\bigr\}.
 \tag{4}
\]
The indices in \(B\) are precisely the breaks, or jumps, in the divisor list: at such an index the next divisor increases by a factor strictly greater than \(2\). Substituting (3) into (1) yields
\[
 a(n)=1+|B|.
 \tag{5}
\]

It remains to show that \(1+|B|\) is exactly the number of maximal contiguous sublists in which every successive term increases by a factor of at most \(2\).

Place a cut between \(d_i\) and \(d_{i+1}\) for every \(i\in B\). These cuts divide the full ordered divisor list into contiguous blocks. Inside any one block there is no cut, so every adjacent pair in that block satisfies
\[
 d_{i+1}\le 2d_i.
\]
Thus every resulting block is \(2\)-dense.

Each such block is maximal. Indeed, if the block has a preceding divisor, then its left boundary comes from a cut, and adjoining that preceding divisor would introduce an adjacent pair \((d_i,d_{i+1})\) with \(d_{i+1}>2d_i\). Likewise, if the block has a following divisor, its right boundary comes from a cut, and adjoining that following divisor would again introduce a pair violating the factor-of-\(2\) condition. At the beginning or end of the full divisor list there is, of course, no term by which the block could be extended in that direction.

Conversely, every maximal contiguous \(2\)-dense sublist must be one of these blocks. To see this, suppose such a sublist starts at \(d_j\) with \(j>1\). If there were no cut immediately before it, then \(d_j\le 2d_{j-1}\), so one could adjoin \(d_{j-1}\) and still have a contiguous \(2\)-dense sublist, contradicting maximality. Hence either \(j=1\) or there is a cut immediately before \(d_j\). The same argument at the right endpoint shows that the sublist either ends at \(d_r\) or has a cut immediately after its last term. Since there are no cuts in its interior, it is exactly one of the blocks formed by cutting at all indices in \(B\).

A nonempty finite list cut at \(|B|\) positions has exactly \(|B|+1\) blocks. Therefore the number of maximal \(2\)-dense contiguous sublists of the divisors of \(n\) is
\[
 |B|+1.
\]
By (5), this is \(a(n)\).

The case \(n=1\) is included: its divisor list is \([1]\), there are no consecutive pairs and hence no cuts, and the unique one-term list is the sole maximal \(2\)-dense sublist; both sides equal \(1\). Thus, for every \(n\ge 1\), \(a(n)\) is exactly the number of maximal contiguous sublists of the divisors of \(n\) whose consecutive terms increase by a factor of at most \(2\).
